name: Tinkerbell
description:
I need an adult-only home with ex-breeder experience that can show me love.

I need a resident dog to help me feel safe but I haven’t met cats yet so I'm not sure

I would like a secure garden to spend time in.

I am learning to walk on a harness but may need more time as I heal.

Please be patient with me, I'm nervous and learning everything from scratch.

I have been spayed and am ready for my forever home.

Tinkerbell has come to us from a breeder and has now settling nicely into foster. She is an extremely hand-shy little girl who is still finding the world a very scary place and will run away and hide in the smallest of spaces when she feels worried. Her new family will need to be prepared to make adjustments around the home to ensure she stays safe while she learns to feel more comfortable. Although she still has a long way to go, Tinkerbell is beginning to show more interest in where her foster family are and what they are doing, which is a lovely little step forward for this precious girl.

Tinkerbell loves her food and treats, although she isn't quite ready to take them from your hand just yet. She gets on wonderfully with the other dogs in her foster home and is also happy to share her space with cats. Having a kind and confident resident dog will be very important for Tinkerbell, as she will need a canine friend to help guide her and give her reassurance as she learns about home life.

Tinkerbell has never lived in a home before, so everything is completely new to her. House training is still ongoing, and her adopters will need to be patient and understanding as she gradually learns all the usual household routines. She will need a very experienced, adult-only home with people who understand extremely worried ex-breeding dogs and appreciate that building trust will be a long journey. She is not yet a little dog who is ready to enjoy lots of handling and cuddles, so her family will need to let her settle at her own pace without putting pressure on her.

Tinkerbell will also need regular grooming to keep her coat comfortable, and her adopters must be prepared to continue this patiently with an experienced and understanding groomer. She has already made progress during her time with us, and we hope that, with the right support, she will continue to discover that life can be a safe and happy place.

Tinkerbell is a truly special little girl who deserves someone willing to see her potential and give her the time she needs to blossom. She will need a very special forever home, but with patience, understanding and a kind canine companion by her side, we hope she will gradually grow in confidence and become the wonderful companion we know she can be.

We've had this little girl with us for nearly a month now and it's clear to see that she's going to need a special forever home with someone who understands that it's going to be a long journey to get this little darling to become the dog we now she can become.

At the moment she's still extremely handsome shy and will run away and hide in the smallest of places which will mean adjusting your house around for her safety. So far in foster Tinkerbell is starting to show interest in where you are and what your up to. She love her food and treats although she won't take them from your hand just yet she gets on great with all our other dogs and doesn't mind the cats either. Bearing in mind she's never been in a home before so everything is new to her so toilet training is ongoing.

Potential adopters will also need to be aware of grooming needs

In the past month I’ve seen more progress in Tinkerbell than ever, and it makes me sooooo happy and proud!!! A little while ago, out of nowhere, she jumped up onto the bench next to me and then quickly jumped back down. It was as if she was thinking “oh gosh, what did I just do!?” … but then she kept doing it again, and again. And now it’s like a little ritual that we have! I eat my lunch with her kennel in the yard nearly every day and because she’s so foodie, she jumps up next to me and waits to see what I have to share. It may or may not be the favourite part of my days!

Another big step for Tinkerbell is that we’ve moved forward with her harness training. I’ve started attaching a lead to it when she’s in the play yard so it trails behind her. A lot of scared dogs get freaked out by this, but it doesn’t seem to bother Tinks at all. I have attempted to pick the lead up twice to essentially ‘walk’ her, and she did panic at the tension, so I’m going to have to ease into it slowly. With dogs as frightened as Tinks, harness training is a huge step, so in my opinion it doesn’t matter how long it takes to get there. What matters is how we get there … slowly, gently, kindly.The last “win” in the past month came a couple of weeks ago. I picked her up in the back of the kennel to put her harness on (which she is not a fan of), and I put her down on my lap to make it easier for me to clip it up. For the first time ever, she just stayed put. She stayed sitting on my lap for about 2 or 3 minutes while I gently stroked her, not holding her in any way - she chose to stay. This made me SO happy and it was such a lovely moment to share with her.Tinks may still be against human touch, but the progress she’s made since her arrival is quite incredible. She really needs someone to take a chance on her now. She deserves it so much.

This week at the rescue we’ve had a big heatwave which resulted in a lot of our dogs needing to be shaved, including my beautiful Tinkerbell as she started to struggle having quite a thick coat. She has the most beautiful fur and she keeps herself so clean and dry, but it had to come off for her comfort. She was taken into the vets to be sedated again, but only because the weather has been so warm.. it would have been too hot to put her through the stress of shaving her all off with no sedation. I have been taking her into the grooming room regularly to brush her and trim the hair around her eyes, and she does definitely get better and better each time, so this is a good sign!! The next time she’s due a shave, I will try again without taking her into the vets to see how she does.

Even though Tinks is still a nervous girl, especially around people she doesn’t know, she is still progressing slowly and steadily. She’s still very reliant on other dogs and tends to copy them a lot of the time, so this has been good for her learning to trust me. She’s watched so many other dogs come up to me for a fuss, take treats from me, and just be comfortable in general being around me, and she is following suit.. just at her own pace. And that’s okay!

She is SUCH a sweet girl who has clearly been through a lot, and it’s not her fault she has such a strong guard up. I absolutely adore working with her and I understand and accept her for who she is. Seeing her get excited over toys and treats, and greeting me with a waggy tail in the mornings really makes me smile, and it gives me hope for her future. She deserves adopters who will love and cherish her the way she always should have been, regardless of if the feelings are mutual.. but I do think she is capable of loving and trusting.. she just needs to find herself with the right people.

Over the last few weeks, our lovely Tinks has reached a huge milestone. After seeing how well she has been progressing with her handling, we felt it was time to take the next step — harness training.

For a dog who finds handling so worrying, we knew there was a strong chance she might not accept wearing a harness. But unless we try, we’ll never know.

Tinks’ other kennel mummy and I took her into the grooming room, where we carefully introduced and fitted her harness. As expected, she was a little unsure and understandably a bit overwhelmed, but she made us both incredibly proud with how she coped. The next step was returning her to her kennel to see how she would manage wearing it throughout the day. Many of our more worried dogs will freeze or refuse to move in this situation, but not our Tinks. She carried on with her day as normal, moving around comfortably with the harness on.

To some, this might not seem like a huge achievement, but for Tinkerbell, it is a massive step in the right direction. Over the coming weeks, we will continue to build on this by practicing daily, with the hope that we can eventually begin introducing a lead in the yard.

With a dog like Tinkerbell, progress takes time, patience, and understanding. Thankfully, she has all of that in abundance, and we will never give up on her.

Tinkerbell has settled into my routine at the rescue beautifully now, so I’m finally starting to see glimpses of the real her. Her guard is definitely still up, but it has dropped slightly and I can tell she’s a lot more comfortable being around me than she used to be. She still won’t allow me to touch her and will bolt away if I go towards her, but she’s approaching me to sniff my fingers, sometimes give me kisses, and taking treats from me every single day now. She also feels content enough to lay near me when I’m sat in the yard eating my lunch, often with her back towards me which I guess is a sign that she does trust me!

One thing she has improved massively with is being picked up. I mentioned in my last update I still had to use a thick blanket and she would still sometimes try to bite (just not as often), but that’s even better again now. This week I was able to pick her up with no blanket, which is HUGE for Tinks!!

Because of how much better she had gotten, I thought I would attempt a full groom - going into it with absolutely no expectations. She allowed me to shave her back, but that’s as far as we could get. She started to get more and more stressed and I really didn’t want to push her and ruin the work we’ve done, so I took her into the vets so she could be sedated to complete the groom. So, she’s now shaved (minus her INCREDIBLE eyelashes), and I think she looks absolutely beautiful. Now that we’ve started fresh with her coat, I’m going to start taking her into the grooming room just once a week or so, and gently brush her etc to get her more used to it all.

Tinkerbell has made slow and steady progress since she’s been on my section and I’m so proud of how brave she’s trying to be. I can tell she wants to come out of her shell a bit more and join in with the rest of the dogs, but she’s not there just quite yet. Something big did happen last week though!! During dinner time I was hand feeding one of her friends, and Tinks came over and started licking the food off my hand for the first time!!!! I was absolutely over the moon and so happy that she felt comfortable enough to do that. Since then she’s done it nearly every day and has also started to take treats from me too if they’re yummy enough. I know this probably won’t sound like a lot to most people, but for a dog like Tinberbell it’s huge. For me, taking food from my hand is usually the first step in earning trust with my scared dogs, so I think we’re heading in the right direction.

We have also made a small amount of progress with Tinkerbell’s fear of being picked up. She still doesn’t like it - at all - but she’s not panicking as much any more and definitely doesn’t try to bite me as much as she did before. I still have to use a thick blanket and be very slow and calm with her, but I think she is starting to slowly realise that I’m not going to hurt her. I trimmed her fringe again a few days ago as her hair seems to grow quite quickly, so I took this opportunity to stroke her head gently for a little while once I was done. She actually started to close her eyes after a minute or so and I think she may have been enjoying it, or at least I hope she was.I adore this little lady and I’m going to do everything I can to show her what love and kindness is. I just hope a special someone will come along and feel the same way about her soon.

Tinkerbell has recently been moved to my section, as she struggles a great deal with being touched and handled by us humans. At present, she goes into complete panic mode whenever I go to pick her up, and she will try to bite to protect herself. This doesn’t mean she’s a nasty dog at all; she’s literally just so scared she will do anything she can to stop it happening. Once I have her comfortably in my arms, she will actually settle really well and will allow me to do things such as give her a gentle fuss and trim the hair on her face. I think the initial picking up is what scares her the most so this is what we’ll work on slowly together.

Tinkerbell is going to need a very experienced home with people who have had terrified dogs before. She’s going to need a lot of work and TLC put into her, and also a lot of understanding. Her adopters will need to accept the fact that she may never be a normal dog, and she may never be a dog who wants fusses or cuddles, but love her anyway. She’s a very special girl, and she needs a home equally as special to help her and give her what she needs.

I’m going to work as closely as I can with her over the next couple of weeks, and hopefully I can earn her trust and prove to her that she doesn’t need to be afraid of me. I’ll keep you all updated!

Tinkerbell has come to us from a breeder and can be a little unsure at first. She is touch-sensitive and may need time to feel comfortable, but once she calms down, she begins to show her gentle, sweet side. Tinkerbell will need an adult-only home that can handle her sassy personality and provide the patience she needs to settle in at her own pace.

She will also need a kind and confident resident dog to guide her and take her under their wing as she adjusts. Tinkerbell is looking for someone to teach her about trust, companionship, and the joys of home life.

As she has never lived in a home before, her adopters will need to be gentle and understanding while she learns about house training and walking on a lead. Starting with a few gentle garden sniffs will be perfect for her confidence as she begins to explore her new world.

Tinkerbell is a little gem who, with time and love, will grow into a devoted and affectionate companion.

name: Toast
description:
I would like a quiet, adult-only home where I can settle in at my own pace.

I need a resident dog to help me feel safe. I live with a cat in my foster home.

I would like a secure garden to spend time in (6ft+)

I enjoy my walks but hate putting my harness on. I need more practice. Go slow please

I will need to learn about house training and practice lead walking

Toast is a delicate little girl who came to us from a breeder and has been slowly finding her confidence in the world. She has been in foster since April and has come a long way, although she is not your average ex-breeder and still has some very specific challenges that her future family will need to understand.

Toast remains extremely nervous about being touched and will avoid handling wherever possible. She can become overwhelmed if she feels pressured, so fitting her harness is still very much a case of careful timing and patience, as she will try to hide if given the opportunity. Her foster mummy has found that this can be tricky, and her new family will need to be experienced and prepared to work within her limits rather than forcing interaction.

Interestingly, once Toast is out on a walk, she absolutely loves it! She walks happily and enjoys saying hello to other dogs, often approaching them with a lovely waggy tail. She has also become much more confident when visiting friends, happily running around with other dogs and enjoying herself. This is a wonderful contrast to how nervous she can be when it comes to being handled.

Toast has also been to the groomers a couple of times and has tolerated this quite happily. She has even allowed her foster mummy to pick her up and cuddle her afterwards, which shows that she is capable of accepting handling in certain situations when she feels comfortable and secure.

Toast is currently living with a cat in her foster home and can live with a dog-savvy cat who respects her space.

She will need a quiet, adult-only home with experienced adopters who understand nervous ex-breeding dogs and can support her without expectation or pressure. A calm, predictable environment will be essential for her ongoing confidence building. Her future family will need to accept that Toast may never become a cuddly or lap dog. She is a little character who likes to do her own thing, and her happiness and confidence will be far more important than expecting her to enjoy affection.

Toast is still learning about house training, and seems to be clean in the home when her foster mummy is around but can have a few accidents when she is left alone. Her new family will need to continue her toilet training patiently as she settles into her new routine.

She will need a kind, confident resident dog in her new home to help guide her and provide reassurance as she adjusts to home life. Having other dogs around clearly brings Toast confidence, and she enjoys their company when out and about and when visiting friends.

Toast arrived with a low-grade luxating patella on her left side, which does not currently cause her any problems, although a disclaimer will need to be signed on adoption. She has also been treated for mucky ears, right-sided otitis, hot spots and dermatitis. She requires Apoquel twice daily for allergies that cause her to itch, and her general health will need to continue to be monitored in her new home.

Behind her nervousness is a gorgeous, mischievous and very cheeky little dog with a huge personality. Toast loves her walks, enjoys the company of other dogs and is clearly a very happy girl when she is out enjoying herself. She may never be the dog who wants to curl up on your lap, but for the right person, watching her confidence grow and seeing her enjoy life will be incredibly rewarding. She will need an experienced home that understands ex-breeder dogs, a kind resident dog to help her settle, and someone who will love her exactly as she is.

This is the gorgeous, mischievous, and very cheeky Toast, or Toastie as she's called in foster. She has been in foster since April and she has come a long way, but is not your average ex-breeder. She still doesn't like to be touched and will avoid this at all costs, meaning putting a harness on is very much trial and error and catching her off guard, meaning before she can find a hiding place that's difficult to get her out of. The strange thing is, once she is out on a walk, she loves it. Saying hello to the other dogs with her waggy tail, she'll even go up to some of the owners with her tail held up high. She happily goes to visit friends with me and loves it, running in and out with the other dogs and even playing with some of the toys they have. Toastie has been to the groomers a couple of times and tolerates this quite happily and, when I go to pick her up, she's happy to be cuddled and carried back to the car. I dread to think what has happened to Toastie in her past life that prevents her from accepting that hands can be gentle and well-meaning.

Toastie does require Apoquel twice daily as she has allergies causing her to itch. She's on Arden Grange Sensitive kibble and Pro Plan Mousse, and this all helps to alleviate the scratching. She has a low-grade luxating patella, although this doesn't cause her any problems at all, but she does have a Disclaimer that would need to be signed when being adopted.

Toastie is a real little character and loves to jump around barking at you with a grin on her face, especially when it comes to having her food, and I'm reminded at every mealtime to hurry up and put hers down. She is a lovely dog but likes to do her own thing. I'm not sure she'll ever be a cuddly or lap dog, but she's happy, and it's just so rewarding when you see her out on her walks, but frustrating that you cannot explain that walkies does mean a harness and lead is required.

Anyone wishing to adopt this little girl really needs experience with ex-breeders and all the problems that can come with them. Toastie is only 4 and will need a resident dog to help her adjust and someone who can accept that she may never be a cuddly lap dog but would love her anyway.

Toast has arrived in Foster and continues to be a very frightened little girl and can panic easily if anyone tries to pick her up, so she really doesn’t cope well with handling at this stage. Once she is settled in her bed, she is a little more comfortable and will allow gentle strokes and will accept quiet reassurance and talking.

She is extremely nervous overall and will need a quiet, adult-only home with experienced adopters who understand how to support a dog like her at her own pace, without pressure. She is also currently living with a cat in her foster home.

I can't believe toast has been here so long that she was due another haircut with me!She has come on tremendously for handling and as long as you're gentle she is content with being picked up, as well as having a harness put on. She is on the journey of learning to walk on a lead and it shouldn't be long before she achieves it.

I've worked with Toast for a while now and I have been able to see how much she's grown over time, especially when it comes to being groomed. The bath is still not her favourite place to be, but she tolerates it, and I think she quite enjoys the warm air of the dryer. She ends up with such a cute haircut because she is so well behaved when it comes to the styling.

This small dog has such a big and beautiful personality and I believe in the right home with another confidence dog she will flourish tremendously.

Toast was such a nervous girl when she came in and she has come on really far since then. I had the pleasure of giving her a much needed groom and although she was nervous she took to it like a champ. She will need grooming upkeep in her forever home to look after her evergrowing locks and I think with a few more pampers she will feel so much more comfortable with it.

She's currently having harness training so she can be more comfortable with the sensation and has gotten much better at being picked up and handled although she can still be a bit jumpy at times but once she's in your arms she's quite calm. She still has a ways to go but I'm so proud of her progress so far and can't wait for when she flourishes with her forever family.

Toast is a delicate little girl who has come to us from a breeder to start her journey towards a brighter future. Right now, the world feels like a very big and scary place to her, and her first instinct is to run and hide in her bed. However, once in your arms, she is easy to handle and accepts gentle reassurance with quiet trust.

Toast will need a calm and understanding home with patient adopters who can give her all the time she needs to find her feet. A kind and confident resident dog will be essential to help guide her, show her that the world can be safe, and give her the courage to explore new experiences.

As she has never lived inside a home before, everything will be new to her, from walking on a lead to learning about house training and family life. Gentle encouragement and plenty of love will help her begin to understand how wonderful it feels to be part of a home.

Toast arrived with a low-grade (Grade 1) luxating patella on the left side, which may improve with gentle exercise. She is also being treated for mucky ears and right-sided otitis as well as dermatitis.

Toast may be shy now, but behind those worried eyes is a sweet girl who just needs the right people to help her shine. With kindness, patience, and a little guidance, she will blossom into a loving and loyal companion.

This dog can be homed with a resident dog.

name: Paris
description:
I'd like a quiet, experienced, adult-only home to help me relax and feel safe.

I need a doggy friend in my new home. I haven’t met cats so I’m unsure.

I haven't tried walks yet, a secure garden will be fine for now.

Please be patient with me, I need to learn house training and lead walking.

I am spayed and ready to find my forever home.

30-09-26 Paris is a scared girly who is not used to being handled. She has come into our care from a breeder in search of a new start and is not a fan of human touch at the moment.

When we have needed to get close to Paris for health checks, we have had to carefully corner her so that we can pick her up. She panics and shakes, but she does allow us to handle her and, once she is safely in our arms, she eventually cuddles into us and allows us to carry out her checks. This shows us that although she is very frightened, she is beginning to understand that we are not going to hurt her.

Paris will need another kind and confident dog in her new home, and this dog will be a much-needed support system for her as she settles in and starts to find her confidence.

As Paris has never lived in a home before, she will need to learn all about house training, lead training and the other basics of home life. She will need an ex-breeding experienced, adult-only home with adopters who understand just how much patience and reassurance she will need.

Paris is a very worried little girl right now, but once she is given the security of being held, we can see that there is a much softer side to her. We hope that with time, patience and the support of a reassuring canine companion, she will slowly learn to trust and enjoy the happy new start she deserves.

Paris has been given the Gift of Life by Margaret Hunter

name: Pippin
description:
I can live with older, dog savvy teenagers, aged 13+ who respect my space.

I need a doggy friend in my new home. I haven’t met cats so I’m unsure.

I'd like a secure garden to potter around in.

I haven't tried walks yet, a secure garden will be fine for now.

Please be patient with me, I need to learn house training and lead walking.

I will be spayed before finding my forever home!

30-09-26 Pippin is a scared girly who has come into our care from a breeder in search of a new start. She will run away from us if she can, but when we do manage to get her into our arms, she settles and allows us to handle her. She is still very unsure of people and her new surroundings, so she will need plenty of patience and gentle encouragement as she begins to learn that she is safe.

Pippin gets on wonderfully with her kennel friends and relies on their company for comfort, so she will need a kind resident dog in her new home to help guide her and give her the reassurance she needs as she settles in and finds her paws. She can live with older, dog-savvy children aged 13+ who are sensible and allow her time to settle in.

As Pippin has never lived in a home before, she will need to learn all about house training, lead training and the other basics of home life. Her new family will need to give her plenty of time to adjust and allow her to progress at her own pace.

We think Pippin will be quite a lively little girl once she has found her confidence and feels comfortable in her surroundings. There is likely to be a fun little personality waiting to emerge underneath all those worries, and we hope that with the support of a lovely canine companion and a patient family, she will slowly blossom into the happy girl she has the potential to be.

Pippin has been given the Gift of Life by Margaret Hunter

name: Juice
description:
I need a calm and quiet, adult only home where I can settle in at my own pace.

I need a resident dog to help me settle in and I have never met cats.

I would like a secure garden to spend time in.

I have learned how to walk on a lead and am enjoying going for walks.

I am in a foster home now so am learning all about home life and house training.

I have had 7 teeth extracted at the time of my spay.

Juice came to us from a breeder and when she first arrived, she was understandably very shy and overwhelmed by everything around her. She wanted to trust people but was nervous about approaching, often hovering nearby and watching with interest before her worries got the better of her. She has since moved into foster and has made some lovely progress and is settling in well. Juice is still cautious, but she now follows her fosterers around the house and will approach for fuss when they offer their hand to her. She particularly loves belly rubs and will completely relax and close her eyes!

Juice will be looking for a calm and quiet, adult only home with adopters who have experience with scared ex-breeding dogs and who will allow her to settle in at her own pace. She will need another kind and confident resident dog in her new home who can take her under their wing and help her settle into her new home. Although she does rely on other dogs for comfort, she can guard her bed from other dogs, particularly when she has just woken up, so she will need a calm, relaxed resident dog who will not disturb her while she is sleeping. She can also be startled by people when she is in her bed and on one occasion she did nip her fosterer when they stroked her in her bed. Her new family will therefore need to be confident managing this behaviour, recognising her body language and ensuring she is always left undisturbed when she is resting.

Juice had never lived in a home before moving to foster, but she is already settling in wonderfully. Her toilet training is going really well and she has only had 2 accidents in the home so far. She has also learned all about walking on a lead and harness and is now becoming more confident wearing her harness and she is starting to enjoy her walks. She is also beginning to understand that the home is a safe place, happily relaxing and sleeping near her fosterers and enjoying the company of their resident dog.

Juice will be looking for an adult-only home with experienced adopters who understand that she is still learning to trust and who will allow her to continue building her confidence at her own pace. She has already come such a long way in a short time, and we hope that with the right family, she will continue to blossom into a happy and loving companion.

She has had 7 teeth extracted at the time of her spay.

Juice has been given the Gift of Life by Holly Kantolinna

Juice has settled in really well. She is still cautious but follows us around the house although backs off if we approach her as she prefers it if you put your hand out to her. She will then approach us, sniff our hand and accept fuss and scratches. She loves having scratches but her favourite are belly rubs and she will close her eyes and completely relax!

She sleeps well over night in her bed on the floor in our bedroom and will wake us up by walking around the room when she needs to go to toilet. Her toilet training is going really well and apart from 2 accidents early on she goes in the garden either asking to go out or when the back door is open taking herself out to go.

She is getting more confident having her harness on for walk and as long as you put it on slowly, she is happy to have it on. She is starting to walk really well on her lead and enjoys her walks and plenty of sniffs! She has met a few dogs on her walks and as long as they are not too energetic and boisterous she seems happy to meet them and have a sniff! She is ok walking along roads but does startle if there are any loud or sudden noises.

She loves being with us in the house and although she doesn't sit right next to us she enjoys being close by and really relaxes and sleeps. She enjoys being with our resident dog but is also happy to follow us outside or sit with us when our dog isn't there. She's also happy travelling in the car with our dog.

She hasn't mastered going up and down stairs yet so at present we are carrying her up and down. She is starting to go up a few small steps on her walks.

She enjoys her food and will sometimes take treats or food from our hands.  She is a lovely girl who has really progressed in the short time that we have had her and is continuing to develop her confidence.

Juice will need an experienced, adult only home with adopters who can understand and manage her nervousness and recognise when she needs space. She can guard her bed from other dogs, particularly when she has just woken up, so any resident dog will need to be calm and relaxed and not likely to bother her while she is sleeping. She can also be startled by people when she is in her bed and, on one occasion, she did nip when she was stroked resting. Her adopters will therefore need to be confident in managing this behaviour, ensuring she is left undisturbed in her bed and giving her the space she needs to feel safe and comfortable.

Juice has come to us from a breeder and is now looking for a loving forever home where she can begin the next chapter of her life.

She is a wonderful little lady who is feeling a little shy and overwhelmed at the moment, but she is trying so hard to be brave. Juice is already showing lovely signs that she wants to trust people. She will quietly hover nearby, watching you with interest and looking as though she would really like to come over for a gentle fuss, but at the last moment her worries get the better of her. We think that with time, patience, love and plenty of reassurance, her confidence will continue to grow and her true personality will begin to shine through.

Juice will be looking for a calm and quiet, adult only home where she can settle in at her own pace. She will need patient adopters who understand that building trust takes time and who will let her make progress without putting any pressure on her. She will also need another kind and confident resident dog in her new home who can be her friend and help show her that life is full of good things.

As Juice has never lived in a home before, everything will be a brand new experience for her. She will need help with housetraining, learning about household routines and gradually becoming accustomed to all the sights and sounds of family life. She is also yet to learn how to walk on a lead and harness, so her adopters will need to introduce this gently and positively as her confidence grows.

Juice is a lovely girl with so much potential. With a patient family by her side and a canine friend to guide her, we are sure she will blossom into a happy and much-loved companion.

name: Milo
description:
I will need an adult-only home that understands me.

I will need to be the only dog in my new home, so all of the attention is on me!

I will need an extra secure garden, at least 6ft+ where I will be safe!

I walk well on a lead but will need my adopters to be understanding of my needs!

I have lived in a home before so may I may already know the basics.

I will be neutered before finding my forever home!

06-10-26 Milo is a super sweet boy who has come to us from a home through no fault of his own. Sadly, he has already been through more changes than a young dog should have to, and he is understandably a little worried in new environments. He takes a lot of comfort from people he knows, but once he feels comfortable, his fun and affectionate personality really starts to shine.

Milo is an incredibly sweet boy who absolutely loves being close to his people and thinks he is the perfect lap dog! He is happiest when he can have a cuddle and will happily climb up for a lap sit. He is a sensitive little soul and will need a kind and patient home where he can continue to build his confidence and learn that he is safe and secure.

Milo will be looking for a home where he can be the only dog and get all the fuss and attention for himself. We are told that he has had a previous incident with a cat and so he cannot be homed with cats or small furries and must be kept on lead unless in a secure area.

Milo has missed out on some socialisation, but he is currently working on his social skills and is making lovely progress. He can happily walk alongside calm dogs and has had some nice greetings. He doesn't always know what to make of other dogs yet and can sometimes get a little carried away when mixing, but with continued positive socialisation we are sure his confidence will grow. He can also react if another dog barks at him first while on lead, so his new family will need to understand this and help him learn how to navigate these situations.

Milo will need an adult-only home with people who have experience of bull breeds and understand what sensitive souls they can be.Although he is a wonderful boy, he would not be suitable for a first time dog owner.He will need a kind and patient family who can give him time to settle and continue building his confidence. He will also need the time he is left home alone built up gradually as he settles into his new home.

Milo will need an extra secure garden of at least 6ft to keep him safe, as he is a young and active boy who could be an escape artist if given the opportunity.

Milo is such a lovely young boy who has already been through so much change. With the right family, patience and continued socialisation, we know he will make a wonderful companion and be the loving, fun little lap dog he is so desperate to be.

name: Sky
description:
I can live with older, calm teens aged, 13+ who allow me time to settle in.

I need a doggy friend in my new home. I haven’t met cats so I’m unsure.

I'd like a secure garden to potter around in.

I walk well on lead but I can be spooked. Let's take it slow!

I haven't tried walks yet, a secure garden will be fine for now.

I am underweight and healing from mastitis. Please read below for more!

Sky is an outrageously beautiful little Poodle cross who has come to us from a breeder and is now settling into foster life. She was incredibly frightened when she first arrived, but has made lovely progress and is becoming much more comfortable with people. She is now happy to be handled and will come looking for fuss when she feels confident. Sky can still be startled by things around her, but she settles well with gentle reassurance and is learning that the world isn't such a scary place.

Sky is a social little girl who loves the company of other dogs and will need a kind and confident resident dog in her new home to help her continue building her confidence. She will suit a quiet household with experienced adopters who understand nervous ex-breeding dogs and will give her the time she needs to settle without putting pressure on her. We would consider a home with sensible, dog-savvy teenagers aged 13+ who will respect her need for space.

Sky is learning about house training in her foster home and will need her new family to continue this patiently. She walks well on a lead, and we would love to see her continue developing this skill with her adopters.

Sky arrived underweight and with mastitis and bilateral dermatitis. She has been healing well, but will need a nutritious diet to help her maintain a healthy weight, and her skin will need continued cleaning and monitoring.

Sky has come such a long way and is showing us more of her lovely personality as she grows in confidence. With a calm home, a kind canine companion and plenty of patience, we believe this beautiful girl will continue to blossom.

Sky has been given the Gift of Life by Ruth Butterworth

Sky is an outrageously beautiful poodle cross. When she came to us, she was petrified. She was terrified of humans, hid in the back of the kennel, and would only eat if she was shut in the back (it was her safe space). To be able to get close enough to touch her felt impossible.

With time, Sky has really come out of her shell. She’s still nervous, especially of new people; however, we have cuddles now. I am a trusted person in her eyes. With time, you could be too.

As she now allows me to stroke her, cuddle her and pick her up, we decided she’d made enough progress to go for a walk.

I fitted her with a harness, leaded her and her kennel friend up (so she’d have a confident friend for guidance) and, to my surprise, she walked like she’d been doing it for years! Noises scared her a little, so did the lead when she pulled it tight. She likes the slack. Other than that, perfect.

I’m so proud of this girl. The progress I’ve seen her make is incredible. Seeing where she is now compared to when I first met her, it genuinely brings a tear (of joy) to my eye.

Sky is a ridiculously beautiful, small poodle cross. She definitely needs a resident dog to keep the progress flowing. Are you the home for Sky? Read the rest of her profile above to get a fuller picture.

Sky is a very scared little lady who has come into our care from a breeder in search of a new start. She can be skittish and quite shut down at the moment so she will need a calm home. Sky prefers to hide at the back of her kennel and finds handling very frightening. She trembles when she is being handled and can't wait to be safely back on the floor, where she will quickly run back to her bed. We know she doesn't understand yet that we are here to help her, so she will need lots of time and patience to learn that she is safe.

Sky will need another kind and confident dog in the home, and this dog will be a much-needed support system for her. Having a friendly dog by her side should help her feel more secure and give her someone to follow as she begins to discover the world outside the kennel.

As Sky has never lived in a home before, she will need to learn all about house training, lead training, and the other basics of home life. Her adopters will need to be very patient and allow her to take everything at her own pace.

We are looking for a quiet, patient home for Sky so that she can relax and settle into her new surroundings without too much hustle and bustle. She will need adopters who understand scared ex-breeding dogs and who are prepared to give her the time she needs without putting any pressure on her. She can live with older, dog-savvy teens, aged 13+ who are sensible and will allow her time to settle in at her own pace.

Sky has arrived very underweight and with mastitis. She is healing well so far, but will need a nutritious diet to help her reach and maintain a healthy weight going forward. She has bilateral dermatitis that will need to be cleaned. This will need to be continued in her new home, and her adopters will need to keep an eye on her progress.

Sky has a long way to go, but underneath all that fear is a little dog who deserves the chance to feel safe and loved. With the right home, a kind canine companion and lots of patience, we hope she will slowly begin to blossom and discover how wonderful life can be.

name: Orange
description:
I need a calm and quiet home where I can settle in at my own pace.

I need a resident dog to help me settle in and I have never met cats.

I would like a secure garden to spend time in.

I am learning to walk on a lead, but it's still very new for me.

I have never lived in a home so I will need help to learn house training.

I have been spayed, and have had a lump removed on my eyelid.

21-09-26 Orange has come to us from a breeder to find her forever home. She is a very sweet girl who is understandably nervous and feeling overwhelmed by all the changes in her life. She is in need of lots of love, patience and TLC as she begins to settle in and understand that she is safe. We feel that with time and kindness, Orange will truly blossom.

Orange will be looking for a calm and quiet home with adopters who have experience with ex-breeding dogs and understand that she will need time and patience to settle in at her own pace. She will need at least one other kind and confident resident dog in her new home to be her friend, give her reassurance and take her under their wing. Having a confident canine companion will help Orange to feel more secure as she learns about her new life. We would consider homing her with gentle, dog savvy teenagers 16+.

Orange has never lived in a home before, so her adopters will need to be kind and understanding as she learns all about home life and new skills such as house training. She has started learning to walk on a lead and harness, but this is still very new to her and she finds it quite worrying at the moment. She will need plenty more gentle practice, and having a confident dog walking alongside her will help to boost her confidence and show her that there is nothing to be afraid of.

Orange is a lovely girl with so much potential, and we hope that once she feels safe and settled, we will get to see her sweet personality shine. She just needs a patient family who will give her the time, love and reassurance she needs to blossom into the happy girl we know she can be.

Orange has had a lump removed from her eyelid during spay, and had a cyst that has been dealt with by our vets at the time of the spay.

name: Rachel
description:
I need a calm and quiet, adult only home where I can settle in at my own pace.

I will need a kind resident dog to take me under their wing. I have never met cats.

I will need a secure garden while I get used to my new home.

I have never been on walks, but may be too scared and will need some time.

I am in a foster home now so am learning all about home life and house training.

I have had a pea size cyst removed from my right shoulder at the time of spay.

Rachel is a very scared girl who has come to us from a breeder. When she first arrived she was extremely overwhelmed by her new surroundings and clearly hadn’t had much socialisation or handling before. Since being with us, she has slowly started to show small signs of progress as she begins to realise she is safe. Although she still finds being handled very frightening, her kennel mum can now stroke her gently when she's in her bed at the back of the kennel.

She will need a calm and quiet adult-only homewith adopters experienced with traumatised ex-breeding dogs who can provide the reassurance and stability she needs to continue building her confidence and learning about trust and kindness. Her adopters will need to allow her to settle in at her own pace and let her set the speed of her progress as she can still become easily overwhelmed.

Rachel relies on other dogs for comfort and reassurance and will need at least one other kind and confident resident dog in her new home who can take her under their wing and help her settle into her new home. They will need to be happy to snuggle up with her and to let her rely on them for support. For some reason she is especially fond of Dachshunds, but she does love all dogs. When she forms a bond with another dog, she absolutely dotes on them and becomes the most loyal best friend to them. It’s so sweet to see.

Day to day, she is a super happy and laid back girl. She LOVES toys and spends a lot of her time chewing on a bone or playing with a plush teddy in one of her beds. She also really loves her food and this has been a great help in gaining her trust and forming a bond with her.

Rachel has never lived in a home before, so she will need very patient and understanding adopters while she settles in and learns all about home life and new skills like house training.She follows a daily routine beautifully, happily running out to the exercise yards and returning to her kennel when it is time to come back in. She is not currently 100% kennel clean, but she is likely to take to toilet training well in a home, as she toilets almost immediately when she goes out into the yard. Her adopters will need to give her plenty of opportunities to go outside while she learns the new routine. Rachel doesn't walk on a lead or harness just yet, but hopefully in the future this is something that we can introduce to her.

The big wide world still feels quite scary for Rachel, but she is beginning to show curiosity in safe environments, and gentle time in the garden will be a great way to help her slowly explore and build confidence. She is not yet cat tested, but we feel cats are unlikely to be an issue for her, although this would need to be assessed appropriately.

Although Rachel has been making progress and will now allow her kennel mum to gently stroke her when she's in a bed in the back of her kennel, she still doesn't enjoy this. She finds being picked up extremely frightening and will panic and does have the potential to bite purely out of fear, so it is imperative that her adopters fully understand her behaviour and are confident managing her needs. We really don’t think she’ll be this way forever, and she’ll get better and better as time goes on, but it would be a lot easier if she was in a home with someone who knew how to help her.

Recently, Rachel needed to have her thick coat clipped during the warm weather, which unfortunately had to be done under sedation as she is not yet ready to be groomed. Despite how frightening this experience must have been for her, she coped far better than we ever expected, allowing herself to be carried to the vets and held for her injection once she was safely in our arms. We couldn't have been prouder of how brave she was. As her coat grows back, we will continue gently introducing her to grooming so she can slowly learn that being brushed doesn't have to be scary.

Rachel has so much potential and, with time, patience and kindness, we truly believe she will continue to make progress and learn that she is safe and loved. She really is an easy dog to care for in every other aspect – she is wonderful with other dogs, thrives on routine and never puts a paw wrong. She just needs a truly understanding home where she can continue building on the trust she has started to develop and finally blossom into the dog she is meant to be.

Rachel came to us with a pea-sized cyst on her shoulder, which was removed at the time of her spay.

Rachel has been given the Gift of Life by Tracy Davidson

Rachel is doing so much better than we expected and is already showing us little glimpses of the lovely girl she could become. She quickly discovered the dog sofas and has found her favourite spot, where she is happiest relaxing alongside her support Dachshund.

Rachel really loves the Dachshunds in the home and will need to be rehomed with at least one calm, friendly and tolerant Dachshund who she can rely on. She is very attached to them and will look for her friend if they are out of sight. She will even approach her fosterer if her Dachshund is sitting on their knee!

Rachel is becoming more inquisitive and has started to approach for a little nose bump on a finger. She will sometimes allow a hand to be offered to her while she is on the sofa and will give a little finger bump in return. She is still not comfortable with being stroked and made it clear that having her face touched was too much for her, so this is something that will need to be respected and worked on slowly.

Rachel is very observant of the other dogs and watches their interactions with people closely. She is still a very scared girl, but she has already exceeded expectations and is beginning to blossom in her foster home. She is happy to share her space with people as long as they do not get too close, and she is even starting to follow basic instructions such as going inside and moving between rooms.

Rachel is settled downstairs in an open crate in the kitchen alongside two Dachshunds and is happy to settle without making any noise. She can be a little destructive with the mats when left for short periods, but overall she is making wonderful progress. We are so pleased to see her beginning to feel safer and more curious about the world around her.

Rachel (or Rachy as I call her) has had quite a few updates on her page now, so I thought I’d do something a little different with this one and basically summarise her and the type of home she needs!

Rachy is a super happy and laid back girl day to day. She LOVES toys and spends a lot of her time chewing on a bone or playing with a plush teddy in one of her beds. She also loves other dogs - especially Dachshunds!! We have no idea why, but she lights up when she’s around them. When she forms a bond with another dog, she absolutely dotes on them and becomes the most loyal best friend to them. It’s so sweet to see. She also loves her food (probably more than anything), and this has been a massive help in gaining her trust and forming a bond with her. She runs to the play yard from her kennel, and back in with no problems, and she also toilets as soon as she gets to the yard every time, so I have a feeling it won’t take long to house train her at all.

Rachy is very easy to look after at the rescue and follows routine beautifully. If you didn’t know anything about her, she looks like quite a normal and happy dog most of the time. But, and this is a big but, she still absolutely hates being touched, and hates being picked up or handled even more. I’ve taken things very slow with her as she isn’t the type of dog you can rush, so I’ve managed to get to the point with her where I can give her gentle strokes when she’s in one of her beds in the back of the kennel. She doesn’t enjoy it, but she does tolerate it now. Picking her up, on the other hand, is a different story. She’s still not used to it and she will still bite to protect herself, so I do have to use a thick blanket to avoid that. I really don’t think she’ll be this way forever, and I do think she’ll get better and better as time goes on, but it would be a lot easier if she was in a home with someone who knew how to help her.

Things such as walking on a lead, grooming, vet visits etc. won’t come easy, but I do believe she will get there and allow these things in the future. She really just needs someone who will love her for who she is, accept her worries and fears, and work with her on them. Most importantly, she needs someone who will never give up on her no matter what.

Rachel’s progress continues slowly and steadily and even though she still doesn’t like to be touched, she is so much more content and calm in general. She’s now more than happy to hang out with me and lay down near me, and just this week she actually went to sleep next to me with her tummy exposed!!! I know that may not sound like a lot, but it’s HUGE for a dog like Rachel with such severe trust issues.

The past couple of weeks at the rescue have been extremely warm and Rachel started to struggle a little bit with having such thick fur, so I decided to get it shaved off. Rachel is still not ready to be groomed, so I did have to take her into the vets to be sedated. This is the first time I’ve had to actually pick her up since I started going the crate and touch work with her, but it had to be done. She does still try her very best to get away and she does still try to bite, but it is less severe than what it was when she first came in. Getting her into my arms was the most difficult part, but after I had hold of her I was able to walk over to the vets carrying her, and hold her while she had her injection without a fuss. I was so, so proud of her. She’s now a bit bald, but so much more comfortable and cooler. When her fur starts to grow back I am going to start introducing her to a brush so she can get used to it, as her coat does grow quite fast and it’s very dense which means it gets matted easily. It’s not ideal for a dog like Rachel needing to be groomed regularly, but I’ll try my very best to ease her into it.

Looking after Rachel on a daily basis is very easy. She follows routine beautifully - running to the play yards and back into her kennel when it’s time to come in. She tries her best to be clean with her toileting and I think if she had access to a garden regularly, she would pick it up really quickly. She also shares everything with her kennel friends perfectly and she never puts a paw wrong with other dogs. Aside from hating being touched, she really isn’t a problem at all. I really am hoping that she’ll start to get used to it soon, and I think she will … but being in a home would help massively. So I hope she doesn’t have to wait too much longer for that to happen.

For the past month, Rachel has officially been my “project dog”. This means I’ve been spending a lot more time working directly with her, and I set a goal for both of us when I started. Because Rachel’s biggest fear is human hands, that became my main focus — helping her feel more comfortable with being touched and gently stroked.

In the first week, I wanted to get her used to my touch without her panicking. When Rachel thinks she’s about to be handled, she’ll run around the kennel, jumping from bed to bed to avoid me, and will bite to protect herself if I get too close. I felt that all the running and panic was only reinforcing her fear, making things harder for both of us. So, I introduced a crate to safely contain her in a smaller space, allowing me to begin gentle handling in a more controlled way.

My hope was that she would start to realise that a soft fuss on her head or body isn’t actually that scary — that the anticipation was worse than the reality. Each day for that first week, I set up a crate at the back of her kennel and spent a short session gently touching her, just once a day to ease her into it.

On the first day, it took a little while for her to go into the crate, but she eventually went in with her friend. She was actually very good and allowed me to gently stroke her face for a few minutes, before becoming a little unsettled and starting to nibble my hand. By the second day, she went into the crate much more quickly and again allowed strokes around her head and under her ears. As I carefully moved further down her body, she became uncomfortable and nibbled a bit harder to let me know she’d had enough.

By the third day, she went straight into the crate, and I focused more on her body. She allowed longer strokes before becoming unsettled. The fourth day was very similar, but on the fifth day there was a real breakthrough — she let me stroke her tummy and chest without any nibbles at all.

After every session, I made sure to sit at the front of her kennel for a few minutes and give her treats so we always ended on a positive note (and to make sure she was still my friend!). Rachel is known to hold a grudge, so maintaining that trust was really important, and thankfully this work hasn’t damaged our relationship at all.

In week two, my goal was to remove the crate and see if she would choose to stay settled in a bed while I handled her. I wasn’t sure how it would go, but she absolutely amazed me. On the first day, she settled into a bed at the back of the kennel while I sat on the floor and gently shuffled towards her — and she stayed still, allowing me to stroke her. I kept things consistent over the next few days without pushing her too far.

By the fifth day, I introduced something new: scissors around her head. She needs a fringe trim, so I wanted to begin desensitising her to the sensation and presence of them. She did incredibly well — so well, in fact, that I managed to snip a tiny bit, which I hadn’t even planned to do. Because she was coping so calmly, I took the opportunity, and it paid off.

In week three, I continued trimming her fringe gradually, little by little. After a few days, I was able to clear the hair from around her eyes.

That’s where we are now. There’s still a long way to go, and Rachel will need plenty more time, patience and love, but I’m so pleased with how far she’s come. We’ve definitely made real progress, and I’m excited to keep building on it with her.

Rachel has been at the rescue for just over a month now and in that time she’s gained a lot of inner confidence, and has blossomed into a very cheeky and happy girl who always seems to be up to mischief!! She absolutely loves toys and gets very excited when I put them in her kennel every morning, and she also loves playing with them in the yards. She’s also very partial to starting ‘parties’ AKA getting all the dogs to have a massive game of chase with her, which she finds very amusing. Her favourite thing in the world though … food!!! She is one of the foodiest dogs I’ve ever met and is always at the front of the queue for breakfast, dinner, and treats.Even though Rachel has made progress in many areas, one thing she still simply can’t handle is being touched by us humans in any way. Her fear of our hands is so strong and she will try to bite to protect herself. This doesn’t mean she’s a nasty dog in any way, it’s just complete panic and fear. It’s something I’m trying to de-sensitise her to and I’m working with her as much as I can, but I do think it’s going to take a long time and a lot of consistency. We don’t know what she’s been through in her life that’s made her the way she is, so all we can do now is prove to her that humans can be kind, and hope that one day she’s able to put her past behind her.Rachel will need a very experienced home with people who will be extremely patient with her, understand her, and work with her through her worries and fears. She’ll need at least 1 resident dog to learn from, and absolutely no children. Things that are normal to most dogs such as going for a walk, being brushed/groomed, or even just having a little fuss, are alien to Rachel, so it’s important her adopters take all of this into consideration and be okay with it.

It may be a long and slow road to get Rachel to where she needs to be, but I promise it will be so worth it. There is no better feeling than a dog like her showing you love and trust for the first time!

Rachel is a very scared girl who has come to us from a breeder. She is a very scared girl at the moment who is quite overwhelmed to find herself here and clearly hasn't had much socialisation before. She is looking for a home with adopters with experience of scared ex-breeding dogs who can provide the reassurance and stability she needs to help build her confidence as she learns about safety, trust, and our intentions.

She will need an adult-only home that can offer a calm and predictable environment where she can take things at her own pace. Rachel will also need at least one kind and confident resident dog to help her settle in and take her under their wing, as she can be easily overwhelmed at the moment.

Rachel has never lived in a home before, so she will need patient and understanding adopters while she learns about house training and how to walk on a lead. Right now, the big wide world may feel too overwhelming for her, so gentle sniffs in the garden would be a good place to start.

Rachel is only acting out of fear, and we have not yet been able to see the girl she will become once she feels safe. She deserves so much love, she just isn’t sure how to accept it yet and will need a truly understanding home to help her blossom.

Rachel has come to us with a pea sized cyst on her shoulder that has been removed at the time of her spay.

name: Candy
description:
I would like a home filled with love and kindness!

I can live with larger, playful resident dogs, or I can be the only dog in the home!

I would like a large, and secure garden with 6ft+ fences.

I walk well on a lead, but I can be strong so my adopters will need to work with this

I have never lived in a home so I will need help to learn house training.

I am spayed and ready to find my forever home! Read below for more!

Candy is a very sweet and affectionate lady who has come to us from a breeder and is now searching for her forever home. She absolutely adores attention and cuddles and, once she gets to know you, it doesn't take her long to show just how loving she really is. Candy simply wants to be close to her people and has completely stolen the hearts of everyone she has met. She has blossomed into the most loving girl and will make a wonderful companion and is sure to become the ultimate cuddle bug in the home.

Candy has built a lovely bond with the staff member who has worked closely with her since she first arrived. She truly trusts her and has come on so much since arriving with us. Candy has such a sweet nature and it is clear how much she enjoys spending time with people she knows and trusts.

Her lead walking has improved so much too. She is now walking much better and really enjoys her outings, although her adopters will need to continue working on her lead manners so she can enjoy plenty of adventures.

Candy mixes well with polite, well mannered dogs however she can sometimes be a little selective with choosing her friends. She doesn’t appreciate when dogs are over the top but when she does make a new friend her own play style can be quite full on! She comes away when called so we are always able to calm her down for a tasty treat. Because of her size and excitable nature, she would not be able to live with smaller breeds of dogs in the home and will need a home without cats.

As Candy is a very large lady, it is important that her adopters have experience with a similar breed and understand her needs. We have found that she can be particularly worried by formal handling, such as veterinary examinations, and finds these situations quite stressful. We will be muzzle training Candy so that she can be safely and comfortably handled for occasions such as vet visits. She recently needed to visit the vet due to sore ears and, although she found having her ears examined uncomfortable, she coped very well with the support of people she knows and trusts. She did also need to visit the vet for a check up on a day when her regular person wasn't around and found it much harder to cope with and became extremely stressed and agitated. She takes so much comfort from her known and trusted people.

Candy would be best suited to an adult-only home where her adopters can give her the time and space she needs to build trust and settle in.

Candy has arrived with a scab on the right side of her face that will be addressed during the time of her spay and is being treated for a ear infection.

Candy has come such a long way since arriving with us and is now so ready for a loving home of her own. She is an absolute angel and a true credit to her breed, with so much love and affection to give. She truly deserves someone who will give her the love, patience and happiness she deserves.

Candy will need more than one meet and greet with her prospective adopters to allow her time to build a bond and feel comfortable with them before being adopted.

Candy has been given the Gift of Life by Carolina Olsen

Candy is an absolute angel and a true credit to her breed. I’ve worked with her since she first arrived at the rescue, and over that time we’ve built such a lovely bond. She truly trusts me and knows that I only have her best interests at heart.

Candy has blossomed into the most loving and affectionate girl, and I genuinely love spending my days with her. She has such a sweet nature and has come on so much since arriving with us.

Candy recently had a vet visit due to having sore ears. Although you could tell she was uncomfortable while the vet was examining them, she was such a good girl throughout, and I was incredibly proud of her.

She has also mixed with quite a few dogs here at the rescue and has been brilliant with all of them. She can sometimes be a little bouncy and excitable when first meeting new dogs, but she listens when asked to calm down and is learning to manage her excitement really well.

Her lead walking has improved so much too, and she’s now walking much better and enjoying her outings.

Candy has come such a long way and is so ready for a loving home of her own. She truly deserves someone who will give her the love, patience and happiness she deserves.

Candy is a very sweet and affectionate lady who has come to us from a breeder and is now searching for her forever home. She absolutely adores attention and cuddles and, once she gets to know you, it doesn't take her long to show just how loving she really is. Candy simply wants to be close to her people and has completely stolen the hearts of everyone she has met. She will make a wonderful companion and is sure to become the ultimate cuddle bug in the home.

Candy can walk on a lead, although she can be quite strong, so her adopters will need to be prepared to continue her training and help her develop her lead manners so she can enjoy plenty of adventures. As she is a very large lady, it is important that her adopters have experience with her breed and understand her needs.

Candy has the confidence to be the only dog in the home, although she could potentially live with another large breed dog following a successful meet and greet. She loves to play and can be quite excitable, so she would not be suitable to live with smaller or more fragile dogs and she will need a home without cats.

Candy is an incredible girl, but she can be sensitive when she is worried or when she feels uncomfortable, for this reason, we feel she would be best suited to an adult-only home where her adopters can give her the time and space she needs to build trust and settle in.

She has arrived with a scab on the right side of her face that will be addressed during the time of her spay.

name: Alice
description:
I need a home that can understand me and provide me with plenty of TLC.

I'd like to live with a resident dog my size and I have never met cats.

I will need a secure garden while I get used to my new home.

I’ve never been on walks before and will need a gentle introduction.

I am in a foster home now so am learning all about home life and house training.

I have been spayed, please read below for more information!

12-10-26 Alice originally came to us from a breeder a few months ago, she was adopted but sadly she struggled to settle into the home and would chose to stay in her crate and wouldn't move freely around the home and so her adopters made the decision to return her to our care after a short adoption. She went straight into a foster home and has now spent two months there settling in.

Alice's foster family have worked patiently to help her build confidence at her own pace. A comfortable dog bed was gradually moved into the busier areas of the house, allowing Alice to become accustomed to everyday family life while still having a safe space of her own.

Initially, Alice found it difficult to remain in a room if her fosterer moved or walked past her. This has improved enormously, and she will now often stay in the room, even when people move around her. In the evenings, she is relaxed enough to settle with the family while they watch television.

Within the home she continues to be “hand shy” unless initiated by herself which is usually a quick lick of your hand.

Out on walks, Alice is an absolute superstar! The moment she sees her lead, she transforms into an excited, happy girl, wagging her tail in anticipation. She is a pleasure to walk alongside her three canine companions, and this is where her confidence and loving nature really shine. When outside on her lead she allows gentle cuddles, takes treats from your hand and is increasingly able to relax and enjoy the world around her. She needs two walks a day to allow for this interaction time.

Alice would love a calm, patient home with one friendly dog of a similar size to help her feel secure and with adopters who have experience with scared ex-breeding dogs. She has shown a particular preference for the Labrador in her foster home, whose companionship she clearly enjoys.

Alice sometimes chooses to sleep away from her fosterers upstairs, but she has a charming way of persuading another dog to settle nearby in the hallway on their beds. Her need for canine companionship is clear, and having a trusted dog friend appears to bring her comfort.

Alice is not looking for a home where everything has to happen at once. She needs a family willing to give her time, reassurance and the freedom to grow in confidence without pressure. She also needs the companionship of another suitable dog and a home where her family are available for regular, gentle interaction throughout the day.

Alice has a continuing journey of discovering trust and the joy that comes with it .

Alice arrived with a cyst on her last mammary gland, which was drained during her spay surgery.

Alice has been given the Gift of Life by Carol Unsworth
